fvq1yb:595: Most agentic architectures work this way today. The harness is a Python process, or possibly a TypeScript process, or some managed framework, that wraps the model. When the agent decides to take an action, the harness translates the tool call into an HTTP request, which triggers something to happen in the backend, such as publishing a queue message or writing to a database. The backend is its own world, separate from the agent. The harness retries at its own pace, the queue retries on its own terms, and the HTTP layer manages its own timeouts. No single trace connects these disparate systems. When something goes wrong, debugging means correlating logs across systems and reconstructing the observed behavior. This is common in backend engineering, but past systems were largely deterministic, while agents are at best only controllable in their randomness. With every agent you add, the probability space expands. The basic scale is agents² × services. In other words, 1 agent with 5 backend systems means 5 random paths to debug. 4 agents with 5 backend systems means 80 random paths to debug. There is no good way to make agents more deterministic. Many of their fundamental capabilities are aimed at giving different answers to similar or even identical inputs. This randomness is not accidental but intentional, because it makes computers useful in an entirely new way. The billion-dollar question is how to create the right harness in the right context to handle agents correctly.

ii4rg6:554: The most important architectural issue in today's AI infrastructure is not about which model to use, but about how much infrastructure is needed to build something truly useful with it. Anthropic, OpenAI, CrewAI, and LangChain all call the layer that wraps the agent a harness. The harness includes orchestration loops, tools (MCP, A2A), memory, context management, and error handling—things that make the model useful. They all agree that the model itself is not the product; infrastructure is. But they differ deeply on how heavy this infrastructure layer should be. Anthropic's harness is thin. It is an elegant loop: assemble a prompt, call the model, execute tool calls, and repeat. Everything is decided by the model. OpenAI adds more structure: instruction stacks, orchestration patterns, and explicit handoff modes. CrewAI adopts a multi-track parallel approach: using deterministic Flows for routing and validation, and leaving the rest to autonomous agents. LangGraph's harness is the heaviest—every decision is a node, every transition is a defined edge, and the entire workflow is encoded in the harness. At one end of this spectrum is strong trust in the model and weak encoding of logic; at the other end is weak trust in the model and strong encoding of logic. Every team building systems with agents must choose how much harness they need. But buried in this debate is an assumption no one questions: the harness lives outside the traditional backend.

Every new language, device, or runtime that implements the primitives interface gets the full system for free: real-time discovery, real-time extension, real-time observability, durable triggers, and calls across everything.
